Neonatal Siberian cranes weigh approximately 121.7 grams [Wwb = approximately 121.7 grams] at hatching, a value that reflects the substantial yolk reserves allocated to the semi-precocial chick during its 29-day incu(29 days [ab = 29 days]) bation period at an average egg temperature of 36.2 °C [T = 36.2 °C]. These altricial newborns exhibit rapid feather growth and are brooded intensively by both parents in the first few weeks following emergence from the egg. The relatively high hatchling mass compared to other crane species is likely an adaptation to the harsh, cold environments of their arctic breeding grounds, providing the chick with greater thermal inertia and energy stores for early development. Hatchlings are capable of coordinated movement within hours but remain completely dependent on parental provisioning for several weeks after their first feeding event.

Field records indicate that under the thermal conditions of the active summer season, with ambient temperatures near 40.4 °C [T = 40.4 °C], the nestling phase culminates in fledging at 76 days after hatching [tx = 76 days after hatching]. This extended period of dependency is typical of large-bodied Gruidae and reflects the substantial time required for the development of flight feathers, the strengthening of flight musculature, and the acquisition of foraging skills through parental guidance. Young birds attain complete flight capability before they achieve nutritional independence, and the post-fledging period is characterized by gradual improvement in foraging efficiency. The fledgling phase is a critical bottleneck in the species' life history, with marked mortality rates observed during the first winter migration among inexperienced young birds that must navigate a complex flyway stretching from northern Siberia to wintering grounds in China and Iran.

Sexual maturation in the Siberian crane is a relatively protracted process, with individuals typically attaining puberty at 228 days after hatching [tp = 228 days after hatching] when maintained under the typical metabolic conditions of the summer active period (40.4 °C [T = 40.4 °C]). This timeline places the onset of gonadal activity well after the first full annual cycle and reflects the substantial somatic growth that must occur before reproductive structures can develop fully. First breeding events are deferred considerably beyond the attainment of puberty, and records from captive populations indicate that the time since birth at first brood is approximately 1040 days [tR = approximately 1040 days] under the same thermal regime of 40.4 °C [T = 40.4 °C]. This two to three year delay before initial reproductive effort is consistent with the slow, K-selected life-history strategy characteristic of large-bodied, long-lived birds.

Adult body mass in this species shows pronounced sexual dimorphism, with ultimate wet weight for males reaching 6166.2 grams [Wwi = 6166.2 grams] while females attain a slightly lower adult body mass of approximately 5283.2 grams [Wwi = approximately 5283.2 grams]. This size disparity, in which males may be over fifteen percent heavier than their female counterparts, is consistent with the pattern observed in many monogamous cranes where male-male competition for breeding territories and defense of nesting sites favors larger body size. Female weight was recorded using a sample of breeding adults from the eastern population during the pre-migration period, while male weights derive from a combination of field measurements and captive records. The dimorphism is most pronounced during the breeding season when males actively defend large territories against conspecifics.

Maximum documented longevity in free-living Siberian cranes is approximately 36.2 years [am = approximately 36.2 years], which translates to roughly 13,213 days of life when considered under the metabolic conditions typical of the species' active period (40.4 °C [T = 40.4 °C]). This remarkable lifespan is consistent with the extreme longevity reported for other Gruidae species and is facilitated by the low annual reproductive output: females typically produce a single clutch of two eggs each year [Ri = two eggs each year], with approximately one successful brood annually [F_R_i = approximately one successful brood annually]. The maximum reproductive rate observed in the species under favorable conditions is thus about two eggs per year, a figure that reflects the intense parental investment required to rear a single precocial chick to independence over the long summer of the tundra.
